analysis.one_liner: Strengthens protections for workers who report unsafe conditions and raises penalties for employers who endanger them.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 1999 with two Democratic sponsors, referred to the Senate labor committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Occupational Safety and Health Act to protect workers who report injuries, illnesses, or unsafe conditions from being fired or disciplined, and to protect workers who refuse a task when they reasonably believe it could cause serious injury. It would set up a faster complaint process run by the Labor Department, with reinstatement, back pay, and damages for workers who are punished for speaking up. It would also extend workplace safety coverage to federal, postal, and (under the bill text) state and local government employees, and sharply raise criminal penalties for employers whose violations seriously harm or kill workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in hazardous jobs, especially those who fear retaliation for reporting injuries or refusing dangerous work; federal, postal, and state and local government employees who currently fall outside OSHA's safety protections; and families of workers killed by willful employer safety violations, who would see far stiffer criminal penalties available.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in dangerous jobs and whistleblowers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal to fire or discipline an employee for reporting an injury, illness, or unsafe condition, and for refusing work the employee reasonably believes would cause serious injury or serious impairment of health [S2][S3].

Gives a worker who is retaliated against 180 days to file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor, requires an investigation and findings within 90 days, and provides for reinstatement, back pay, compensatory damages, exemplary damages, and attorney's fees [S3].
Reinstatement ordered in a preliminary decision cannot be delayed while an employer contests the case [S3].

Extends OSHA employer coverage to the United States, the Postal Service, and any state or political subdivision, which the bill text makes explicit [S3]; the CRS summary describes coverage of federal and postal employees [S2].

Raises criminal penalties for employer safety violations: the maximum prison term for a first conviction rises from six months to ten years, and for repeat convictions from one year to twenty years, with fines set under the federal fine schedule rather than fixed low caps [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those in hazardous industries, who would face damages awards, attorney-fee liability, higher fines, and possible prison terms for willful safety violations; the federal government, which would take on new complaint investigations and coverage of its own and state workforces.

drawbacks.text: Expanded employer liability and criminal exposure raises compliance and legal costs, which critics of OSHA expansion argued could fall on smaller businesses and, through them, on prices and jobs [S3].

Covering state and local government employees would shift enforcement obligations and costs to state and local governments and create a new federal role over workforces historically left to state law [S3].

Criminal prison terms of ten and twenty years for safety violations are a major escalation, and opponents of such measures argue that individual managers can face prosecution for workplace accidents even when responsibility is diffuse [S3].
The bill as introduced never advanced far enough for the committee to consider, amend, or weigh these costs on the record [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker protections address a real gap: the existing OSHA retaliation rule was narrow and slow, and federal employees had no OSHA coverage at all. The costs fall on employers whose practices endanger workers, which is the point, though smaller firms would bear proportionally more compliance burden and the criminal-penalty escalation is aggressive. The larger limitation is that the bill was never debated, so no consensus version of these tradeoffs was ever reached.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone, joined by Senator Edward Kennedy, introduced the bill on March 17, 1999 [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote at any point in the 106th Congress [S5].
The bill had one cosponsor in addition to its sponsor, both Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in hazardous industries, particularly those relying on the weakness of OSHA's retaliation protections and the low criminal penalties for willful safety violations, because nothing changed; workers who face retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions remain under the pre-1999 rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who benefited from unchanged weak protections

sides.party_line_note: No vote or recorded opposition exists; the bill had two Democratic sponsors, one Democratic cosponsor, and died in committee, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, mining)
industries.note: The bill would expose them to retaliation suits with reinstatement, back pay, and damages, plus attorney-fee liability, and prison terms of up to 10 or 20 years for willful violations that injure or kill workers. Workers reporting unsafe conditions would gain the ability to speak up without losing their jobs.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and the U.S. Postal Service
industries.note: They would become OSHA-covered employers subject to inspections, penalties, and retaliation liability for the first time. Their employees would gain safety protections they currently lack.

The bill text would extend OSHA's employer definition to any state or political subdivision, putting their workforces under federal safety enforcement. Their employees would gain protections while the governments take on federal compliance costs.
